USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the tariff posture already in force and restart a negotiation track with Beijing rather than escalating to the threatened additional $267B or rushing further action. Keep the scheduled Jan 1 rise to 25% as standing pressure, and signal willingness to talk once China returns to the table, while pairing this with relief for the farm belt before the midterms.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is real but contained, so I score it +0.3. List 3 (~$200B at 10%, rising to 25% Jan 1) took effect Sept 24, pushing combined Section 301 coverage to ~$250B, while China retaliated the same day with 5-10% tariffs on ~$60B of US goods including soybeans and pork (NPR/BI, 9/18). That retaliation is targeted squarely at the farm belt — the NYT (4/19) and Globe & Mail (9/23) report GOP incumbents and farm groups warning of midterm losses, and even the $12B aid package is described as an insufficient 'mute button' (Des Moines Register, 8/3). Meanwhile US fundamentals remain strong (IP 104.1, consumer sentiment 100.1, dollar firm ~113.7, unemployment lowest since 2000), whereas China's economy is visibly slowing (Shanghai Comp -20% YTD, RMB slide to ~6.88/$). That asymmetry argues against an existential threat reading — but the collapse of the Liu He talks and domestic political exposure to escalating farm retaliation keep this a mild threat, not a clean US opportunity. On action, I recommend a near-neutral +0.15 stance: the US has already applied maximum pressure and retains leverage through the scheduled 25% tier, so escalating further to $267B now would raise consumer costs exactly ahead of the midterms and harden a deadlock, with no talks venue active. De-escalating unilaterally would forfeit hard-won leverage. Holding and re-engaging diplomatically while relieving farmers is the posture most consistent with both the threat level and US leverage.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold our current retaliatory posture and signal readiness to return to talks on equitable terms, without escalating further or making unilateral concessions. Further tariff escalation against a much larger US import base would only invite the threatened 'phase three' coverage of virtually all our exports, and we have pressing domestic reasons — currency depreciation, capital-flow risk, and a slowing economy — to avoid rattling financial markets. We should keep the negotiating channel open (ideally resuming high-level contact once the US shows sincerity) while cushioning the export hit through domestic stimulus and Made-in-China 2025 diversification.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is high and rising: US Section 301 coverage now spans ~$250B of our imports (Lists 1-2-3), with List 3 set to climb from 10% to 25% on Jan 1 2019 and Trump explicitly threatening a further ~$267B (almost all our exports to the US) if we retaliate again (event timeline 09-17, 09-18, 09-24; Politico/CNBC). China has already retaliated to its practical ceiling — $50B equivalent plus $60B at 5-10%, covering 85-95% of US exports to China — precisely because our import base is far smaller than our export base (Business Insider, DW). Macro evidence shows the strain: the yuan has depreciated ~8-10% since April and the PBoC re-introduced the counter-cyclical factor on Aug 24 to defend the currency against capital outflows (CNBC, Belfer), and Beijing is ramping infrastructure stimulus to cushion a slowing economy (Politico). Given our limited symmetry in retaliation and the genuine danger of a self-harming escalation spiral that could trigger phase-three coverage and capital flight, the rational stance is neither maximal escalation (which invites a worse US response) nor unilateral concession (which would set a damaging precedent and undercut credibility). A calibrated hold-plus-negotiate posture — matching where we already are, keeping talks alive on 'equality, integrity and mutual respect' terms, and signaling openness before the Jan 1 25% ratchet — best defends our export economy and financial stability.
